about: After the peace, the boy Gwern goes gladly from one uncle to the next, until Efnysien takes him by the feet and thrusts him headlong into the fire, and the house breaks into battle. The Irish revive their dead in the cauldron of rebirth until Efnysien, lying among the Irish corpses, is thrown in himself and stretches out until the cauldron bursts in four pieces, and his heart with it. Only seven men of the Island of the Mighty escape, and Bendigeidfran, wounded in the foot with a poisoned spear, has his head cut off and gives the seven their road: seven years feasting at Harlech with the Birds of Rhiannon, fourscore years at Gwales in Penfro with the head as good company as ever, and then London, where it is to be buried in the White Hill. Branwen dies of grief on the bank of the Alaw, Caswallon son of Beli has taken the crown, and all goes as foretold until Heilyn son of Gwyn opens the door towards Cornwall and every sorrow comes back at once. The branch closes with Ireland repeopled by five women in a cave and their five sons, and with the list of tales it holds.

sentences.t: Ac yna, guedy daruot y tangneued, galw o Uendigeiduran y mab attaw.
sentences.l: And then, after finishing the peace, calling of Bendigeidfran the boy to-him.
sentences.i: And then, when the peace had been concluded, Bendigeidfran called the boy to him.
sentences.n: The part opens mid-line in Evans col. 55, straight after the kingship is conferred on the boy (y'r mab), with no large initial. guedy daruot y tangneued 'after the peace's being finished': daruot 'happen, come to an end' (modern darfod), the verbal noun whose preterite is daruu (darfu); tangneued 'peace', as at the end of the last part. galw o Uendigeiduran 'calling by Bendigeidfran': the subject of a verbal noun is given with o 'of', and o softens the name (Bendigeiduran > Uendigeiduran, u = f). attaw 'to him' (at conjugated, 3 sg. masc.). The boy is Gwern, now king of Ireland.

sentences.t: Y gan Uendigeiduran y kyrchawd y mab at Uanawydan, a phawb o'r a'e guelei yn y garu.
sentences.l: From Bendigeidfran went the boy to Manawydan, and everyone of those-who him saw loving him.
sentences.i: From Bendigeidfran the boy went to Manawydan, and everyone who saw him loved him.
sentences.n: Y gan 'from (beside)': the phrase comes first, so the verb takes the particle y. kyrchawd 'made for, went to', 3 sg. preterite of kyrchu with the old ending -awd (modern -odd). at Uanawydan ← Manawydan, softened after at. a phawb 'and everyone': pawb with the spirant mutation after a 'and'. o'r a'e guelei 'of all who saw him': o'r a 'of what, of all who', 'e the infixed object 'him', guelei the imperfect of gwelet (gu = gw). yn y garu 'loving him': yn + verbal noun, with y 'his, him' as its object, softening caru > garu — one of the jobs of y.

sentences.t: E gan Uanawydan y gelwis Nyssyen uab Eurosswyd y mab attaw.
sentences.l: From Manawydan called Nisien son of-Euroswydd the boy to-him.
sentences.i: From Manawydan, Nisien son of Euroswydd called the boy to him.
sentences.n: E gan is the same as Y gan above: the scribe often writes e for y. y gelwis 'called', 3 sg. preterite in -is of galw; the i of the ending turns the stem vowel a to e. Then the plain order after a fronted phrase: verb, subject, object. Nyssyen is Nisien, the peaceable brother, as the earlier parts write the name; Eurosswyd is Euroswydd, father of Nisien and Efnysien (ss for s; the final d is dd). uab ← mab, softened between two names. Three uncles in turn — Bendigeidfran, Manawydan, Nisien — make much of the new king.

sentences.t: Y mab a aeth attaw yn diryon.
sentences.l: The boy it-was-that went to-him fondly.
sentences.i: The boy went to him fondly.
sentences.n: Subject first, then a and the verb: the abnormal sentence, the tale's ordinary narrative order, with nothing stressed. aeth 'went', preterite of mynet. yn diryon 'gently, fondly': tirion 'gentle, kind' softened after the adverbial yn (t > d); the Red Book also has yndiryon. The boy's willingness from uncle to uncle is the courtesy of the hall, and it sets up Efnysien's complaint in the next sentence.

sentences.t: “Paham,” heb yr Efnissyen, “na daw uy nei, uab uy chwaer, attaf i? Kyn ny bei urenhin ar Iwerdon, da oed genhyf i ymtiryoni a'r mab.”
sentences.l: “Why,” said Efnysien, “does-not come my nephew, son of my sister, to-me I? Though he-were not king over Ireland, good it-would-be with-me to-make-friends with the boy.”
sentences.i: “Why,” said Efnysien, “does my nephew, my sister's son, not come to me? Even were he not king over Ireland, I should be glad to make friends with the boy.”
sentences.n: heb yr Efnissyen: heb takes yr before a vowel, y before a consonant (heb y Bendigeiduran next). Efnissyen is Efnysien, the trouble-maker of the earlier parts. na daw 'does not come': daw, 3 sg. present of dyuot, with the negative na used after Paham 'why'. uy nei 'my nephew' (uy = fy; n does not change). attaf i 'to me' (at conjugated, 1 sg.). Kyn ny bei 'though he were not': bei, imperfect subjunctive of bot; urenhin ← brenhin, softened as the predicate after it (Evans's page leaves a space before urenhin, a matter of layout only). da oed genhyf i 'good it would be with me', I would be glad. ymtiryoni a 'make friends with' is ym- + tirion, the word of the last sentence.

sentences.t: “Aet yn llawen,” heb y Bendigeiduran.
sentences.l: “Let-him-go gladly,” said Bendigeidfran.
sentences.i: “Let him go gladly,” said Bendigeidfran.
sentences.n: Aet 'let him go': the 3 sg. imperative of mynet (modern aed). yn llawen 'gladly': the adverbial yn, with llawen 'glad' unchanged, since ll does not soften after yn. heb y before a name beginning with a consonant, as heb y Matholwch in the last part. Bendigeidfran's ready yes is the hinge of the scene: nothing in the hall yet suggests danger.

sentences.t: Y mab a aeth attaw yn llawen.
sentences.l: The boy it-was-that went to-him gladly.
sentences.i: The boy went to him gladly.
sentences.n: The king's words are repeated as narrative: the abnormal sentence again (Y mab a aeth 'the boy went'), and yn llawen carried over from the permission to its keeping. a aeth: the relative-looking a after a subject put first; aeth begins with a vowel, so no mutation shows. The tale lets the boy's gladness stand, without a word of comment, before what follows.

sentences.t: “Y Duw y dygaf uyg kyffes,” heb ynteu yn y uedwl, “ys anhebic a gyflauan gan y tylwyth y wneuthur, a wnaf i yr awr honn.”
sentences.l: “To God I-bear my confession,” said he-for-his-part in his mind, “unlikely it-is [what] outrage by the household to-be-done, that I-will-do the hour this.”
sentences.i: “To God I make my confession,” he said in his heart, “the household would think it an unlikely outrage, the one I am going to do this very hour.”
sentences.n: Y Duw y dygaf uyg kyffes 'to God I bear my confession', an oath: y 'to' softens Duw, but d also spells dd, so nothing shows; dygaf, 1 sg. present of dwyn; uyg kyffes = fy nghyffes, kyffes with the nasal mutation after uy 'my', written g k. yn y uedwl 'in his mind' ← medwl. ys anhebic 'it is unlikely': ys 'is'. The rest is awkward: a gyflauan (← kyflauan 'outrage, crime', softened after a; the same adjective + a + noun shape as Da a dwy ynys in Branwen's lament below) … y wneuthur (← gwneuthur, softened after y 'to': 'to be done') … a wnaf i 'that I will do' is read as 'the outrage the household would think unlikely to be done — I will do it now'. The Red Book has the same words; the construction is not certain. gan y tylwyth 'in the household's view'. yr awr honn 'this hour'. The oath is the one 004 renders 'by my confession to God' (ym kyffes y Duw); here the Welsh is a full sentence, and the English keeps it as one.

sentences.t: A chyuodi y uynyd, a chymryt y mab erwyd y traet, a heb ohir, na chael o dyn yn y ty gauael arnaw, yny want y mab yn wysc y benn yn y gynneu.
sentences.l: And rising up, and taking the boy by the feet, and without delay, nor getting of any-man in the house a-hold on-him, until he-thrust the boy head-first into the kindling.
sentences.i: And he rose, and took the boy by the feet, and without delay, with no man in the house able to lay hold on him, thrust the boy headlong into the fire.
sentences.n: A chyuodi, a chymryt: verbal nouns for the verbs, each with the spirant after a (kyuodi, kymryt). y uynyd 'upwards' (i fyny): mynyd softened after y 'to'. erwyd y traet 'by the feet': erwyd is herwyd 'by'. heb ohir 'without delay' (gohir softened after heb). na chael o dyn … gauael arnaw 'nor any man getting a hold on him', still governed by heb: o dyn is o ddyn, d spelling dd. The Red Book has kynn kael 'before (any man) got'. yny want 'until he thrust': gwant, 3 sg. preterite of gwanu 'thrust, stab', softened after yny. yn wysc y benn 'head first' (still Welsh yn wysg ei ben): penn softened after y 'his'. yn y gynneu: kynneu 'kindling', here the lit fire; the Red Book has yn y gynneu tan 'into the kindling of fire'. Why kynneu softens after y is not clear.

sentences.t: A fan welas Uranwen y mab yn boeth yn y tan, hi a gynsynwys uwrw neit yn y tan, o'r lle yd oed yn eisted rwng y deu uroder.
sentences.l: And when saw Branwen the boy burning in the fire, she it-was-that made-to throw a-leap into the fire, from the place where she-was sitting between the two brothers.
sentences.i: And when Branwen saw the boy burning in the fire, she made to leap into the fire from where she was sitting between her two brothers.
sentences.n: A fan is a phan 'and when': pan with the spirant after a, the ph written f, as y foen in the last part (the Red Book writes Aphan). welas ← gwelas, softened after pan; Uranwen ← Branwen, softened as the subject straight after the verb. yn boeth 'burning hot' ← poeth after yn. hi a gynsynwys 'she set herself to': -wys preterite of kynsynnyaw 'intend, set oneself to' (cysynio), softened after a; 'made to' is plainly the sense, the exact shade less so. uwrw neit 'to throw a leap', to leap: bwrw softened as the object. yd oed 'she was'. rwng y deu uroder 'between the two brothers' (broder softened after deu): Bendigeidfran and Manawydan.

sentences.t: A chael o Uendigeiduran hi yn y neill law, a'y tarean yn y llaw arall.
sentences.l: And getting of Bendigeidfran her in the one hand, and his shield in the hand other.
sentences.i: And Bendigeidfran caught her in one hand, with his shield in the other.
sentences.n: A chael 'and getting', kael with the spirant after a; o Uendigeiduran marks the subject, as in the first sentence of the part, and hi 'her' is the object. yn y neill law 'in the one hand': llaw softened after neill. In y llaw arall 'the other hand' it is not, because ll does not soften after the article even in a feminine noun. a'y tarean 'and his shield': after the infixed 'y 'his' the soft mutation (a'y darean) would be expected, but tarean stays unsoftened, and the Red Book has the same (ae taryan). tarean here and taryan below are one word, tarian 'shield'.

sentences.t: Ac yna, ymgyuot o bawb ar hyt y ty.
sentences.l: And then, rising-up of everyone along the house.
sentences.i: And then everyone rose up all through the house.
sentences.n: One bare verbal noun is the whole sentence: the uproar is told without a finite verb. ymgyuot 'rising up, starting up together': ym- + kyuot 'rise' (the verbal noun is also kyuodi, as above). o bawb 'of everyone': the subject of the verbal noun, pawb softened after o. ar hyt y ty 'along the house, all through the house'. The hall that was built to hold both hosts now holds a fight.

sentences.t: A llyna y godwrw mwyhaf a uu gan yniuer un ty, pawb yn kymryt y arueu.
sentences.l: And there-is the tumult greatest that was by the company of-one house, everyone taking his arms.
sentences.i: And that was the greatest uproar ever raised by the company of one house, every man taking up his arms.
sentences.n: llyna 'there is, that is' (beside llyma 'here is'), pointing at the scene. y godwrw 'the tumult, din' (godwrdd; the Red Book god6rd), unchanged after the article because it is masculine (a feminine noun would lose its g). mwyhaf 'greatest', superlative of mawr. a uu 'that was': bu softened after the relative a. gan yniuer un ty 'by the company of one house': yniuer 'host, company'. pawb yn kymryt y arueu 'everyone taking his arms': no verb, a subject and yn + verbal noun, as in the last part; y arueu 'his arms' (arfau), a vowel showing no mutation.

sentences.t: Ac yna y dywot Mordwyd Tyllyon, “Guern gwngwch uiwch Uordwyt Tyllyon.”
sentences.l: And then said Morddwyd Tyllion ('Pierced Thigh'), “Gwern gwngwch uiwch Morddwyd Tyllion.”
sentences.i: And then Morddwyd Tyllion said, “Gwern gwngwch uiwch Morddwyd Tyllion.”
sentences.n: y dywot 'said', preterite of dywedut (also dywawt). Mordwyd Tyllyon means 'Pierced Thigh': morddwyd 'thigh' + tyllyon 'holed, pierced', a plural adjective from twll 'hole'. Who bears the name is not said; it may be Bendigeidfran himself or another man. The cry is obscure. Gwern is clear, and Uordwyt ← Mordwyt is softened, perhaps as an address; gwngwch and uiwch are not known as words in this form, and no reading of them is safe, so the cry is left untranslated. Evans prints gwngwch uiwch as two words, as does the Red Book (g6ng6ch ui6ch); the second witness divides gwn, gwchuiwch. The division is Evans's.

sentences.t: Ac yn yd aeth pawb ym pen yr arueu, y kynhelis Bendigeiduran Uranwen y rwng y taryan a'y yscwyd.
sentences.l: And while went everyone to the head of the arms, held Bendigeidfran Branwen between the shield and his shoulder.
sentences.i: And while everyone was making for their weapons, Bendigeidfran held Branwen between his shield and his shoulder.
sentences.n: yn yd aeth is hard to parse; it is read as 'while, as (everyone) went', yn with the particle yd; the Red Book has ac yny aeth. ym pen yr arueu 'to the head of the arms', to take up weapons: ym pen ← yn penn, written ym before p. y kynhelis 'held, sheltered', 3 sg. preterite in -is of kynnal (a > e before the ending). Uranwen ← Branwen, softened as the object straight after the subject. y rwng 'between'. y taryan is unsoftened again, where y daryan would be expected whether y is 'his' or the article, since tarian is feminine (the Red Book has y daryan); a'y yscwyd 'and his shoulder'. Bendigeidfran shields his sister with his own body.

sentences.t: Ac yna y dechrewis y Gwydyl kynneu tan dan y peir dadeni.
sentences.l: And then began the Irish kindling fire under the cauldron of-rebirth.
sentences.i: And then the Irish began to kindle a fire under the cauldron of rebirth.
sentences.n: y dechrewis 'began': dechreuis, the 3 sg. preterite in -is of dechreu, with w written for u; the verb is singular before its plural noun subject, y Gwydyl 'the Irish', the usual rule. kynneu tan 'kindling fire'. dan 'under'. peir dadeni 'cauldron of rebirth': dadeni is dad- 'back, again' + geni 'be born', the g softened after the prefix and so lost. This is the cauldron Bendigeidfran gave Matholwch: the dead put into it rise again.

sentences.t: Ac yna y byrywyt y kalaned yn y peir, yny uei yn llawn, ac y kyuodyn tranoeth y bore yn wyr ymlad kystal a chynt, eithyr na ellynt dywedut.
sentences.l: And then were-thrown the corpses into the cauldron, until it-was full, and they-would-rise next-day [ ] the morning as men of-fighting as-good as before, except that they-could-not speak.
sentences.i: And then the corpses were thrown into the cauldron until it was full, and next morning they would rise up fighting men as good as before, except that they could not speak.
sentences.n: y byrywyt 'were thrown', impersonal preterite (-wyt) of bwrw (the last part has byrwyt). kalaned 'corpses' (celanedd). yny uei 'until it was': bei, imperfect subjunctive, softened after yny. y kyuodyn 'they would rise': kyuodynt, imperfect, with its -t not written (the Red Book kyuodynt), the imperfect of a thing that kept happening. tranoeth y bore 'next day in the morning': the scribe left a blank between tranoeth and y bore; nothing is lost (the Red Book has drannoeth alone). yn wyr ymlad 'as fighting men' ← gwyr after yn. kystal a chynt 'as good as before': kynt with the spirant after a 'as'. na ellynt ← gellynt, imperfect of gallu, softened after na, the g lost.

sentences.t: Ac yna pan welas Efnissyen y calaned heb enni yn un lle o wyr Ynys y Kedyrn, y dywot yn y uedwl, “Oy a Duw,” heb ef, “guae ui uy mot yn achaws y'r wydwic honn o wyr Ynys y Kedyrn;
sentences.l: And then when saw Efnysien the corpses without room in one place of men of-the-Island of-the-Mighty, he-said in his mind, “Oh God,” said he, “woe me, my being the cause of this havoc of men of-the-Island of-the-Mighty;
sentences.i: And then, when Efnysien saw that the dead of the men of the Island of the Mighty had no place anywhere, he said in his heart, “Oh God,” he said, “woe is me, that I am the cause of this havoc among the men of the Island of the Mighty;
sentences.n: heb enni yn un lle is uncertain. enni may be genni 'have room, be contained' (the verb of kynghanei and enghis in the last part), softened after heb with the g lost: the British dead had no place, no cauldron, to go into. Or it may be geni 'be born' (the Red Book writes eni), 'without rebirth', as in dadeni; the point is the same. Oy a Duw 'Oh God'. guae ui 'woe (to) me': ui = fi. uy mot 'my being': bot with the nasal mutation after uy (b > m). yn achaws 'as the cause'. y'r wydwic honn 'of this havoc': wydwic is a rare word, softened after the article and so feminine; 'havoc, slaughter' is guessed from the context. The speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: a meuyl ymi,” heb ef, “ony cheissaf i waret rac hynn.”
sentences.l: and shame to-me,” said he, “unless I-seek I deliverance against this.”
sentences.i: and shame on me,” he said, “if I do not seek some deliverance from this.”
sentences.n: meuyl ymi 'shame to me', the oath of the earlier parts, rendered 'shame on me'; ymi is y 'to' conjugated, 1 sg. (the Red Book has ym). ony cheissaf i 'unless I seek': ony 'if not' gives the spirant, keissaf > cheissaf, as ony chaei in the last part; the present looks to the future. waret ← gwaret 'deliverance, remedy', softened as the object after the verb. rac hynn 'against this'. The second heb ef inside one speech is the tale's habit, not a new speaker.

sentences.t: Ac ymedyryaw ymlith calaned y Gwydyl, a dyuot deu Wydel uonllwm idaw, a'y uwrw yn y peir yn rith Gwydel.
sentences.l: And hiding-himself among the corpses of the Irish, and coming two Irishmen bare-arsed to-him, and his throwing into the cauldron in the guise of-an-Irishman.
sentences.i: And he hid himself among the Irish corpses, and two bare-bottomed Irishmen came to him and threw him into the cauldron for an Irishman.
sentences.n: ymedyryaw is a rare word, a reflexive (ym-) verbal noun; the context asks for 'hide, thrust oneself' among the dead, but the word is not well understood (the Red Book has the same). ymlith 'among' (yn + plith). deu Wydel ← Gwydel, softened after deu. uonllwm ← bonllwm 'bare-bottomed' (bon 'base, bottom' + llwm 'bare'), softened as an adjective after a noun counted by deu: the men who fed the cauldron, presumably stripped for the work. idaw 'to him'. a'y uwrw 'and his throwing': 'y 'him' is the object, softening bwrw. yn rith Gwydel 'in the guise of an Irishman' (rhith 'form, guise').

sentences.t: Emystynnu idaw ynteu yn y peir, yny dyrr y peir yn pedwar dryll, ac yny dyrr y galon ynteu.
sentences.l: Stretching to-him he-for-his-part in the cauldron, until breaks the cauldron into four pieces, and until breaks the heart his-own.
sentences.i: He stretched himself out in the cauldron until the cauldron burst into four pieces, and his own heart burst with it.
sentences.n: Emystynnu is ymestynnu 'stretch oneself' (ym- reflexive), spelt with E-. idaw ynteu 'to him for his part': with a verbal noun, y 'to' can mark the subject, so 'his stretching'. yny dyrr 'until breaks': tyrr, 3 sg. present of torri, softened after yny; a vivid present in past narrative, as yny glyw in the last part. torri here is intransitive, 'break, burst'. yn pedwar dryll 'into four pieces'. y galon ynteu 'his own heart': calon softened after y 'his', ynteu stressing that it was his. The Red Book has y gallon.

sentences.t: Ac o hynny y bu y meint goruot a uu y wyr Ynys y Kedyrn.
sentences.l: And from that was the amount of-victory that was to the men of-the-Island of-the-Mighty.
sentences.i: And that was the source of such victory as the men of the Island of the Mighty had.
sentences.n: The phrase o hynny 'from that' comes first, so the verb takes y: y bu 'was'. y meint goruot 'the amount of victory': meint 'size, amount'. a uu 'that was': bu softened after the relative a. y wyr ← gwyr, softened after y 'to': 'that was to the men', that the men had. The phrasing is dry, since the next sentence says how little the victory came to.

sentences.t: Ny bu oruot o hynny eithyr diang seithwyr, a brathu Bendigeiduran yn y troet a guenwynwaew.
sentences.l: There-was-not victory from that except escaping of seven-men, and wounding Bendigeidfran in the foot with a-poison-spear.
sentences.i: There was no victory in it, save that seven men escaped, and Bendigeidfran was wounded in the foot with a poisoned spear.
sentences.n: Ny bu oruot 'there was no victory': goruot softened after bu. eithyr 'except'. diang 'escaping' is dianc (the Red Book's spelling), -g written for -nc. seithwyr 'seven men' (seith + gwyr, softened in the compound). brathu 'piercing, wounding', with Bendigeiduran its object. a guenwynwaew 'with a poison-spear': gwenwyn 'poison' + gwaew 'spear', whose g softens and is lost in the compound. a 'with' gives the spirant only to c, p, t, so guenwynwaew does not change.

sentences.t: Sef seithwyr a dienghis: Pryderi, Manawydan, Gliuieu Eil Taran, Talyessin, ac Ynawc, Grudyeu uab Muryel, Heilyn uab Gwyn Hen.
sentences.l: That-is the seven-men that escaped: Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifiau Eil Taran, Taliesin, and Ynog, Gruddieu son of-Muriel, Heilyn son of-Gwyn Hen.
sentences.i: The seven who escaped were Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifiau Eil Taran, Taliesin, Ynog, Gruddieu son of Muriel, and Heilyn son of Gwyn Hen.
sentences.n: Sef seithwyr a dienghis 'that is the seven men who escaped', and the names answer it. dienghis, 3 sg. preterite in -is of dianc (a > e before the ending, nc > ngh); the relative verb is singular after a plural antecedent. Pryderi is the son of Pwyll and Rhiannon from the First Branch. Gliuieu Eil Taran: eil is usually taken as 'son, offspring', taran is 'thunder'; the epithet is not certain. Talyessin is Taliesin, the poet of later legend. Ynawc is Ynog, Grudyeu uab Muryel is Gruddieu son of Muriel, and Heilyn uab Gwyn Hen is 'son of Gwyn the Old'. The ac stands before Ynawc, not before the last name; the list is printed as written.

sentences.t: Ac yna y peris Bendigeiduran llad y benn.
sentences.l: And then caused Bendigeidfran cutting-off his head.
sentences.i: And then Bendigeidfran ordered his head to be cut off.
sentences.n: y peris 'caused', 3 sg. preterite of peri, as in the last part; peri + verbal noun is 'have (something) done'. llad is 'strike, cut' as well as 'kill': llad y benn 'cutting off his head', penn softened after y 'his'. The order is the king's own; his charge to the seven follows, and the stroke itself is told after it (y llas y benn ef).

sentences.t: “A chymerwch chwi y penn,” heb ef, “a dygwch hyt y Gwynuryn yn Llundein, a chledwch a'y wyneb ar Freinc ef.
sentences.l: “And take you the head,” said he, “and carry (it) as-far-as the White-Hill in London, and bury (it) with its face towards France it.
sentences.i: “And take the head,” he said, “and carry it to the White Hill in London, and bury it with its face towards France.
sentences.n: A chymerwch, a chledwch: 2 pl. imperatives with the spirant after a (kymerwch, kledwch; cladu has e before -wch). dygwch 'carry', imperative of dwyn; the object is understood. hyt y Gwynuryn 'as far as the White Hill': Gwynuryn is gwyn 'white' + bryn 'hill', the b softened in the compound (u = f). Llundein is London. a'y wyneb … ef 'with its face': a 'with' + 'y … ef 'his, its', the pronoun closing the clause. ar Freinc 'towards France': Ffreinc, F written for ff, which does not mutate. The Red Book has a chledwch yno ef a'e wyneb ar freinc 'bury it there with its face towards France'.

sentences.t: A chwi a uydwch ar y ford yn hir; yn Hardlech y bydwch seith mlyned ar ginyaw, ac Adar Riannon y canu ywch.
sentences.l: And you it-is-that will-be on the road long; in Harlech you-will-be seven years at dinner, and the Birds of-Rhiannon singing to-you.
sentences.i: And you will be long upon the road. At Harlech you will be seven years at the feast, and the Birds of Rhiannon singing to you.
sentences.n: chwi a uydwch 'you will be': bydwch, the future (also habitual) 2 pl. of bot, softened after a; then y bydwch after the fronted yn Hardlech. ar y ford 'on the road': ffordd, f written for ff. Hardlech is Harlech, where the Branch began. seith mlyned 'seven years': blyned with the nasal mutation after seith. ar ginyaw 'at dinner' ← kinyaw, softened after ar. Adar Riannon y canu 'the Birds of Rhiannon singing': y stands here for yn before a verbal noun (the Red Book yn canu). Riannon is Rhiannon of the First Branch. ywch 'to you' (y conjugated, 2 pl.).

sentences.t: A'r penn a uyd kystal gennwch y gedymdeithas ac y bu oreu gennwch, ban uu arnaf i eiryoet.
sentences.l: And the head it-is-that will-be as-good with-you its fellowship as was best with-you, when it-was on-me I ever.
sentences.i: And the head will be as good fellowship to you as ever it was at its best, when it was upon me.
sentences.n: A'r penn a uyd 'and the head will be': byd, the future of bot, softened after a. kystal 'as good', the equative of da; kystal … ac 'as good … as'. y gedymdeithas 'its fellowship': kedymdeithas softened after y 'its'. ac y bu oreu 'as it was best': goreu softened after bu. ban uu arnaf i 'when it was on me': ban = pan, bu softened after it; arnaf 'on me' (ar conjugated, 1 sg.). eiryoet 'ever'. The head will keep company as if it still sat on Bendigeidfran's shoulders.

sentences.t: Ac y Guales ym Penuro y bydwch pedwarugeint mlyned.
sentences.l: And in Gwales in Penfro you-will-be four-score years.
sentences.i: And at Gwales in Penfro you will be fourscore years.
sentences.n: y Guales 'in Gwales': y here stands for yn 'in'. The Red Book writes ygg6ales, that is yng Ngwales with the nasal mutation, which the White Book's spelling does not show (compare y glan Alaw below). Gwales is an island off Penfro (Pembroke), usually identified with Grassholm. ym Penuro 'in Penfro': yn + P is written ym P, the nasal mutation (ym Mhenfro) not shown. pedwarugeint 'four score', eighty (pedwar + ugeint). mlyned again has the nasal mutation after the numeral.

sentences.t: Ac yny agoroch y drws parth ac Aber Henueleu, y tu ar Gernyw, y gellwch uot yno a'r penn yn dilwgyr genhwch.
sentences.l: And until you-open the door towards Aber Henfelen, the side towards Cornwall, you-can be there and the head uncorrupted with-you.
sentences.i: And until you open the door towards Aber Henfelen, on the side that faces Cornwall, you may stay there, and the head will be uncorrupted with you.
sentences.n: yny agoroch 'until you open': agoroch, 2 pl. present subjunctive of agori, the mood used after yny of something still to come. parth ac 'towards' (ac before a vowel). Aber Henueleu: so Evans here and below, and the Red Book here, though the Red Book has henuelen below; the place is Aber Henfelen, and -leu looks like an old slip for -len. y tu ar Gernyw 'the side facing Cornwall': Kernyw softened after ar. y gellwch 'you can'. a'r penn yn dilwgyr 'and the head uncorrupted': di- 'without' + llwgyr 'corruption' (llwgr), the ll softened to l. genhwch 'with you' (gan conjugated, 2 pl.).

sentences.t: Ac o'r pan agoroch y drws hwnnw, ny ellwch uot yno.
sentences.l: And from-the-time you-open that door, you-cannot be there.
sentences.i: But from the time you open that door, you cannot remain there.
sentences.n: o'r pan 'from (the time) when'. agoroch 'you may open' again, the present subjunctive. ny ellwch 'you cannot': gellwch, 2 pl. present of gallu, softened after ny, the g dropping away. uot ← bot 'be', softened as the object of the verb. The prohibition is one of folk-tale: the door, not the clock, sets the limit of their stay, and the next paragraph but one keeps it in view.

sentences.t: Kyrchwch Lundein y gladu y penn. A chyrchwch chwi racoch drwod.”
sentences.l: Make-for London to bury the head. And go you onward across.”
sentences.i: Make for London to bury the head. And go on, across the sea.”
sentences.n: Kyrchwch 'make for', 2 pl. imperative of kyrchu; Lundein ← Llundein, softened as the object straight after the verb. y gladu 'to bury' ← cladu after y 'to'. A chyrchwch chwi racoch drwod 'and go on across': a chyrchwch with the spirant after a; racoch 'before you, onward' (rac conjugated, 2 pl.; the Red Book ragoch); drwod 'across, over', back over the sea to Britain. The second order, to cross, is what they must do first; the speech ends here.

sentences.t: Ac yna y llas y benn ef, ac y kychwynassant a'r penn gantu drwod, y seithwyr hynn, a Branwen yn wythuet.
sentences.l: And then was-struck-off his head he, and they-set-out with the head with-them across, these seven-men, and Branwen as eighth.
sentences.i: And then his head was struck off, and they set out across with the head, these seven men, and Branwen the eighth.
sentences.n: y llas 'was struck off': the impersonal preterite of llad. y benn ef 'his head', y … ef. kychwynassant 'they set out', 3 pl. preterite in -assant. gantu 'with them': written so here, apparently short for gantunt (the Red Book gantunt). drwod 'across'. y seithwyr hynn 'these seven men' is set in apposition at the end, after the verb has already said 'they'. yn wythuet 'as the eighth': wythfed 'eighth', with the predicative yn; w does not mutate.

sentences.t: Ac y Aber Alau yn Tal Ebolyon y doethant y'r tir.
sentences.l: And to Aber Alaw in Tal Ebolion they-came to the land.
sentences.i: And they came ashore at Aber Alaw in Tal Ebolion.
sentences.n: y Aber Alau 'to Aber Alaw': y 'to'; Alau here and Alaw below are one name, the mouth of the river Alaw in Anglesey. Tal Ebolyon is Tal Ebolion, the commote of north-west Anglesey whose name was explained earlier in this branch (mabinogi-005). The phrase comes first, so the verb takes y: y doethant 'they came', 3 pl. preterite of dyuot. y'r tir 'to the land', ashore: the crossing from Ireland is done.

sentences.t: Ac yna eisted a wnaethant, a gorfowys.
sentences.l: And then sitting they-did, and resting.
sentences.i: And then they sat down and rested.
sentences.n: eisted a wnaethant 'sitting they did': the verbal noun first, closed by a wnaethant, the narrative pattern for 'they sat'. a gorfowys 'and resting': gorffwys, f written for ff, a second verbal noun hung on the same a wnaethant; a 'and' does not change g. The Red Book has Ac yno 'and there' for Ac yna 'and then'.

sentences.t: Edrych oheni hitheu ar Iwerdon, ac ar Ynys y Kedyrn, a welei ohonunt.
sentences.l: Looking of-her she-for-her-part on Ireland, and on the Island of-the-Mighty, what she-saw of-them.
sentences.i: She looked at Ireland, and at the Island of the Mighty, as much of them as she could see.
sentences.n: Edrych oheni hitheu 'her looking, she for her part': the subject of the verbal noun is given with o, here conjugated, 3 sg. fem. (oheni), and the pronoun hitheu, as ohonaw ef in the last part. edrych ar 'look at'. a welei ohonunt 'what she saw of them': welei, imperfect of gwelet, 'what she could see'; ohonunt 'of them' (o conjugated, 3 pl.).

sentences.t: “Oy a uab Duw,” heb hi, “guae ni o'm ganedigaeth. Da a dwy ynys a diffeithwyt o'm achaws i.”
sentences.l: “Oh Son of God,” said she, “woe us of my birth. Good [a] two islands were-laid-waste on-account-of-me I.”
sentences.i: “Oh Son of God,” she said, “woe to us that I was ever born! Two good islands have been laid waste because of me.”
sentences.n: Oy a uab Duw 'Oh Son of God': the house's Oy a Duw, with mab softened after the vocative a. guae ni: so Evans prints, plainly; ni is 'we, us', 'woe to us'. The Red Book and the second witness read ui 'me', 'woe is me', which sits better with o'm 'of my' that follows; ni is kept as printed and may be a slip. o'm ganedigaeth 'of my birth': ganedigaeth is a by-form of genedigaeth. Da a dwy ynys is uncertain: the Red Book has ys da dwy ynys 'good are the two islands'; it is taken as 'two good islands', with da put first. a diffeithwyt 'that were laid waste': impersonal preterite of diffeithaw. o'm achaws i 'because of me'.

sentences.t: A dodi ucheneit uawr, a thorri y chalon ar hynny.
sentences.l: And putting a-sigh great, and breaking her heart at that.
sentences.i: And she heaved a great sigh, and her heart broke with it.
sentences.n: dodi ucheneit 'putting a sigh', heaving one: ucheneit 'sigh' is feminine, so mawr after it softens to uawr. a thorri 'and breaking': torri with the spirant after a. y chalon 'her heart': calon with the spirant after y 'her', where y galon above was 'his heart' with the soft mutation; the mutation alone shows whose. ar hynny 'at that, thereupon'. Branwen is the second in this part whose heart breaks, after Efnysien; the phrase comes again with Caradog.

sentences.t: A gwneuthur bed petrual idi, a'e chladu yno y glan Alaw.
sentences.l: And making a-four-sided grave for-her, and her burying there on-the-bank of-Alaw.
sentences.i: And a four-sided grave was made for her, and she was buried there on the bank of the Alaw.
sentences.n: gwneuthur 'making': a 'and' gives the spirant only to c, p, t, so g stays. bed petrual 'a four-sided grave' (petryal 'square, four-cornered'). idi 'for her' (y conjugated, 3 sg. fem.). a'e chladu 'and her burying': 'e 'her' gives the spirant, kladu > chladu. y glan Alaw 'on the bank of Alaw': Evans prints yglan as one word; it is yg 'in' + glan 'bank' with the nasal mutation, that is yng nglan, the mutated ng written g after the preposition yg (the Red Book writes ygglan). The division y glan is ours, following y gwaelawt in the last part; read it as 'in, on the bank'.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny, kerdet a wnaeth y seithwyr parth a Hardlech, a'r penn ganthunt.
sentences.l: And at that, walking did the seven-men towards Harlech, and the head with-them.
sentences.i: And thereupon the seven men went on towards Harlech, with the head.
sentences.n: Ac ar hynny 'and at that, thereupon'. kerdet a wnaeth 'walking did': the verbal-noun pattern, with wnaeth singular before its plural noun subject y seithwyr. parth a Hardlech 'towards Harlech' (a before h, no change). a'r penn ganthunt 'and the head with them', a clause with no verb; ganthunt is gan conjugated, 3 pl. (the scribe writes both ganthunt and gantunt).

sentences.t: Val y bydant y kerdet, llyma gyweithyd yn kyuaruot ac wynt, o wyr a gwraged.
sentences.l: As they-are walking, behold a-company meeting with them, of men and women.
sentences.i: As they went on their way, there met them a company of men and women.
sentences.n: Val y bydant y kerdet 'as they are walking': bydant, the present (habitual) 3 pl. of bot, a vivid present in past narrative; y kerdet stands for yn kerdet, as the Red Book writes it. llyma 'behold' sets the scene with a bare noun: gyweithyd ← kyweithyd 'company, band', softened after llyma, as llyma gennadeu in the last part. yn kyuaruot ac wynt 'meeting with them': yn before a verbal noun does not mutate. o wyr a gwraged 'of men and women': gwyr softened after o; gwraged, after a, does not change.

sentences.t: “A oes gennwch chwi chwedleu?” heb y Manawydan.
sentences.l: “Is-there with-you you news?” said Manawydan.
sentences.i: “Have you any news?” said Manawydan.
sentences.n: A oes 'is there?': A is the question particle, oes the form of 'is' used in questions and denials of existence. gennwch chwi 'with you': gan conjugated (2 pl.) with the pronoun after it; 'is there news with you' is 'have you news'. chwedleu 'news', plural of chwedyl, as in the last part. heb y Manawydan: heb y before the name. The answer starts a new paragraph, as a change of speaker does in this text.

sentences.t: “Nac oes,” heb wynt, “onyt goresgyn o Gaswallawn uab Beli Ynys y Kedyrn, a'y uot yn urenhin coronawc yn Llundein.”
sentences.l: “There-is-not,” said they, “except conquering of Caswallon son of-Beli the Island of-the-Mighty, and his being as king crowned in London.”
sentences.i: “None,” they said, “but that Caswallon son of Beli has conquered the Island of the Mighty, and is crowned king in London.”
sentences.n: Nac oes 'there is not': the answer repeats the verb with the negative nac. onyt 'except, but'. goresgyn o Gaswallawn 'the conquering by Caswallon': the subject with o, Caswallawn softened after it; Ynys y Kedyrn is the object. Caswallon son of Beli is the Cassivellaunus of Roman history as Welsh legend knew him. a'y uot 'and his being': 'y 'his' softens bot. yn urenhin coronawc 'as crowned king': brenhin softened after the predicative yn; coronawc 'crowned' (coron + -awc).

sentences.t: “Pa daruu,” heb wynteu, “y Gradawc uab Bran, a'r seithwyr a edewit y gyt ac ef yn yr ynys honn?”
sentences.l: “What befell,” said they-for-their-part, “to Caradog son of-Brân, and the seven-men that were-left together with him in this island?”
sentences.i: “What became of Caradog son of Brân,” they said, “and the seven men who were left with him in this island?”
sentences.n: Pa daruu 'what befell': daruu, preterite of darfod 'happen', with pa 'what'. heb wynteu 'said they for their part': now the seven speak together. y Gradawc ← Cradawc, softened after y 'to': 'what befell to Caradog'. a edewit 'who were left': impersonal preterite of adaw, as yd edewit in the last part, where Caradog and the stewards were left to keep the island. y gyt ac ef 'together with him'.

sentences.t: “Dyuot Caswallawn am eu penn, a llad y chwegwyr, a thorri ohonaw ynteu Gradawc y galon o aniuyget, am welet y cledyf yn llad y wyr, ac na wydat pwy a'e lladei.
sentences.l: “Coming of-Caswallon upon their head, and killing the six-men, and breaking of-him he Caradog his heart from grief, for seeing the sword killing his men, and that he-did-not-know who it-was-that them was-killing.
sentences.i: “Caswallon fell upon them and killed the six, and Caradog's heart broke for grief at seeing the sword killing his men and not knowing who it was that killed them.
sentences.n: The answer is told in verbal nouns. am eu penn 'about their head', upon them. y chwegwyr 'the six men' (chwech + gwyr). a thorri ohonaw ynteu Gradawc y galon 'and the breaking by him, Caradog, of his heart': the subject is marked with o, conjugated, and Cradawc stands softened in apposition to it. o aniuyget 'from grief': aniuyget is a rare word, 'grief, dismay' by its context; its exact sense is uncertain. am welet 'for seeing' (gwelet softened after am). y wyr ← gwyr 'his men'. na wydat 'that he did not know': gwydat, imperfect of gwybot, softened after na. a'e lladei 'who was killing them': 'e infixed 'them', lladei imperfect.

sentences.t: Caswallawn a daroed idaw wiscaw llen hut amdanaw, ac ny welei neb ef yn llad y gwyr, namyn y cledyf.
sentences.l: Caswallon, it-had-befallen to-him putting a-mantle of-magic about-him, and did-not-see anyone him killing the men, but the sword.
sentences.i: Caswallon had put on a mantle of magic, and no one could see him killing the men, only the sword.
sentences.n: Caswallawn a daroed idaw 'Caswallon, it had befallen him': daroed, the pluperfect of darfod 'happen', with y 'to' and a verbal noun, is the Middle Welsh way of saying 'he had (done)'; Caswallawn stands first as the topic. wiscaw ← gwiscaw 'put on', softened as the subject of daroed (the thing that had befallen him). llen hut 'a mantle of magic': llen 'cloak, veil', hut 'magic, enchantment'. amdanaw 'about him' (am conjugated, 3 sg. masc.). ny welei neb ef 'no one saw him': welei, imperfect of gwelet, softened after ny. namyn 'but, only'.

sentences.t: Ny uynhei Gaswallawn y lad ynteu: y nei, uab y geuynderw, oed.
sentences.l: Did-not-wish Caswallon his killing he-for-his-part: his nephew, son of his cousin, he-was.
sentences.i: Caswallon had no wish to kill Caradog himself: he was his nephew, his cousin's son.
sentences.n: Ny uynhei 'did not wish': mynhei, imperfect of mynnu, softened after ny. Gaswallawn ← Caswallawn, softened as the subject straight after the verb. y lad ynteu 'his killing, him for his part': llad softened after y 'his', the object. y nei, uab y geuynderw, oed 'his nephew, son of his cousin, he was': the predicate first, oed at the end; keuynderw 'first cousin' softened after y 'his'. nei here is a cousin's son, a wider sense than modern 'nephew'.

sentences.t: A hwnnw uu y trydyd dyn a torres y gallon o aniuyget.
sentences.l: And that-one was the third man that broke his heart from grief.
sentences.i: And he was the third man whose heart broke for grief.
sentences.n: hwnnw 'that one', Caradog. uu ← bu, softened as after the relative a, which is not written. y trydyd dyn 'the third man': the tale points to a reckoning of three, in the manner of the triads, of those whose hearts broke for grief; who the other two were is not said here, though Branwen above may be meant as one. a torres 'who broke': torres, preterite of torri, is left unsoftened after the relative a, where a dorres would be expected; the Red Book has the same. y gallon 'his heart', calon softened after y 'his', written with ll here. o aniuyget as before.

sentences.t: Pendarar Dyuet, a oed yn was ieuang gyt a'r seithwyr, a dienghis y'r coet,” heb wynt.
sentences.l: Pendaran Dyfed, who was as a-young lad with the seven-men, it-was-that escaped to the wood,” said they.
sentences.i: Pendaran Dyfed, who was a young lad with the seven, escaped to the forest,” they said.
sentences.n: Pendarar: so Evans prints, and so the Red Book (pendarar); the man is Pendaran Dyfed, the lad who went with the seven stewards in the last part, and the final -r is presumably an old slip. a oed 'who was'. yn was ieuang 'as a young lad': gwas softened after the predicative yn; ieuang is ieuanc with -g. gyt a'r seithwyr 'with the seven men'. a dienghis 'escaped', the -is preterite of dianc, as in the list of the seven above. y'r coet 'to the wood'.

sentences.t: Ac yna y kyrchyssant wynteu Hardlech, ac y dechreussant eisted, ac y dechreuwyt ymdiwallu o uwyt a llynn.
sentences.l: And then made-for they-for-their-part Harlech, and they-began sitting, and was-begun supplying-oneself of food and drink.
sentences.i: And then they made for Harlech, and sat down, and began to take their fill of food and drink.
sentences.n: kyrchyssant 'made for', 3 pl. preterite (-yssant) of kyrchu. dechreussant 'began', 3 pl. preterite. y dechreuwyt 'it was begun': impersonal preterite (-wyt), 'they began' without naming who. ymdiwallu 'supply oneself, take one's fill' (ym- + diwall 'well supplied'). o uwyt 'of food': bwyt softened after o. In Evans the u is a letter raised above the line between o and wyt, an insertion; it is taken into the line here (the second witness agrees). a llynn 'and drink'.

sentences.t: Ac y dechreuyssant wynteu uwyta ac yuet, dyuot tri ederyn, a dechreu canu udunt ryw gerd, ac oc a glywssynt o gerd, diuwyn oed pob un iwrthi hi.
sentences.l: And they-began they-for-their-part eating and drinking, coming three birds, and beginning singing to-them a-kind of song, and of what they-had-heard of song, unlovely was every one beside-it.
sentences.i: And as they began to eat and drink, there came three birds and began to sing them a kind of song, and every song they had ever heard was graceless beside it.
sentences.n: Ac y dechreuyssant … dyuot tri ederyn reads loosely: 'and they began to eat and drink, (and there was) the coming of three birds'; the English supplies 'as'. The second witness prints [gyt ac] 'as soon as' after Ac y; Evans has no such words, nor has the Red Book, and they are not supplied. uwyta ← bwyta, softened after the verb. ryw gerd 'a kind of song': kerd softened after ryw. oc a glywssynt 'of all that they had heard': glywssynt, pluperfect (-ssynt) of clywet, softened after a. diuwyn 'unpleasing' (di- + mwyn 'gentle, pleasant'). iwrthi hi 'beside it' (y wrth, conjugated, fem., for kerd).

sentences.t: A fell dremynt oed udunt y guelet uch benn y weilgi allan.
sentences.l: And far sight it-was to-them their seeing above the head of the sea out.
sentences.i: And it was a far sight for them to see the birds, away out over the sea.
sentences.n: A fell is a phell 'and far': pell with the spirant after a, ph written f, as A fan above. dremynt ← tremynt 'sight', softened after the adjective pell set before it. oed udunt 'was to them'. y guelet 'their seeing': y here is 'their' (eu, as the Red Book writes it), which does not mutate, so gwelet stays. uch benn y weilgi 'above the sea': penn softened after uch, gweilgi after the article. allan 'out', far off.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny o gin— A chyn amlyket oed udunt wy a chyn bydynt gyt ac wy.
sentences.l: And at that of din— And as clear it-was to-them they as if they-were together with them.
sentences.i: And at that fea— And they were as plain to them as if they had been there beside them.
sentences.n: The first words are a scribe's false start. Evans col. 58, the last line of a leaf, ends Ac ar hynny o gin; col. 59 opens A chyn amlyket … and then gives Ac ar hynny o ginyaw … in full. The scribe began the next sentence too soon, broke off, and wrote it again in its place; it is not a catchword, and the Red Book has the words once. It is printed as written, with a dash: read past it. A chyn amlyket 'and as clear': kyn + amlyket, the equative of amlwc 'clear, plain', with the spirant after a. a chyn bydynt 'as if they were': a 'as' completes the equative, kyn 'though, as if'; bydynt is the habitual past of bot. gyt ac wy 'with them'.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny o ginyaw y buant seith mlyned.
sentences.l: And at that of dinner they-were seven years.
sentences.i: And at that feast they spent seven years.
sentences.n: This is the sentence the scribe began too soon. ar hynny o ginyaw 'at that (much) of dinner', at that feast: kinyaw softened after o. y buant 'they were', 3 pl. preterite of bot, with y after the fronted phrase. seith mlyned, with the nasal mutation after seith. It is as Bendigeidfran foretold: seven years at Harlech, with the Birds of Rhiannon singing.

sentences.t: Ac ym penn y seithuet ulwydyn, y kychwynyssant parth a Gualas ym Penuro.
sentences.l: And at the end of the seventh year, they-set-out towards Gwales in Penfro.
sentences.i: And at the end of the seventh year they set out for Gwales in Penfro.
sentences.n: ym penn 'at the end of': yn + penn, written ym before p. y seithuet ulwydyn 'the seventh year': blwydyn is feminine, so it softens after the ordinal with the article. y kychwynyssant 'they set out', 3 pl. preterite, with y after the fronted phrase. parth a 'towards'. Gualas is Gwales, spelt so here (the Red Book g6alas too), Guales in Bendigeidfran's charge. ym Penuro as above.

sentences.t: Ac yno yd oed udunt lle teg brenhineid uch benn y weilgi, ac yneuad uawr oed, ac y'r neuad y kyrchyssant.
sentences.l: And there was for-them a-place fair royal above the head of the sea, and a-hall great it-was, and to the hall they-made-for.
sentences.i: And there they had a fair and kingly place above the sea, and it was a great hall, and into the hall they went.
sentences.n: yd oed udunt 'there was for them', they had: yd before a vowel, after the fronted yno. lle teg brenhineid 'a fair royal place': brenhineid 'kingly', from brenhin. yneuad 'hall' is neuad with a y before it, kept as one word as in the earlier parts; uawr ← mawr, softened after the feminine noun. ac yneuad uawr oed 'and a great hall it was': the predicate first, with no a before oed (the Red Book has ac yneuad uawr a oed yno udunt). y'r neuad y kyrchyssant 'to the hall they made', the phrase first.

sentences.t: A deu drws a welynt yn agoret; y trydyd drws oed y gayat, yr hwnn y tu a Chernyw.
sentences.l: And two doors it-was-that they-saw open; the third door was shut, the one the side towards Cornwall.
sentences.i: And they saw two doors standing open; the third door was shut, the one on the side towards Cornwall.
sentences.n: deu drws a welynt 'two doors they saw': the object first, then a and welynt, the imperfect 3 pl. of gwelet. yn agoret 'open'. y gayat 'shut': y here is the predicative yn, which softens kayat 'shut' (caead); the Red Book writes yngayat. yr hwnn 'the one'. y tu a Chernyw 'the side towards Cornwall': Kernyw with the spirant after a 'towards'. This is the door of Bendigeidfran's warning.

sentences.t: “Weldy racco,” heb y Manawydan, “y drws ny dylywn ni y agori.”
sentences.l: “See-you yonder,” said Manawydan, “the door we-ought-not its opening.”
sentences.i: “See there,” said Manawydan, “the door we must not open.”
sentences.n: Weldy 'see you, look': gwel, imperative of gwelet, with the pronoun di 'you' joined to it and the g lost, as in wele 'behold' (the Red Book weldi). racco 'yonder'. ny dylywn ni 'we ought not': 1 pl. present of dylyu 'owe, ought' (-wn is the 1 pl. present ending). y agori 'its opening', to open it: y 'its' before a vowel, so nothing mutates. The relative pronoun is not written: y drws ny dylywn 'the door (that) we ought not'. Manawydan, whose branch comes next, already plays the cautious one.

sentences.t: A'r nos honno y buant yno yn diwall, ac yn digrif ganthunt.
sentences.l: And that night they-were there in-plenty, and merry with-them.
sentences.i: And that night they were there in plenty, and took their pleasure.
sentences.n: A'r nos honno 'and that night', the phrase first, so y buant 'they were'. yn diwall 'in plenty, well supplied' and yn digrif 'pleasant, merry': diwall and digrif are softened after the predicative yn, but d also spells dd, so the change does not show. ganthunt 'with them': digrif ganthunt 'pleasant to them', they took pleasure in it, the adjective of the house word digrifwch 'amusement'.

sentences.t: Ac yr a welsynt o ouut yn y gwyd, ac yr a gewssynt e hun, ny doy gof udunt wy dim, nac o hynny nac o alar yn y byt.
sentences.l: And for-all that they-had-seen of grief in their presence, and that they-had-got themselves, there-did-not-come memory to-them they of-anything, neither of that nor of sorrow in the world.
sentences.i: And for all the grief they had seen before their eyes, and had suffered themselves, they remembered nothing of it, neither that nor any sorrow in the world.
sentences.n: yr a welsynt 'for all that they had seen': yr is er 'despite, for all', and a the relative 'what'; welsynt, pluperfect (-synt) of gwelet. o ouut 'of grief': gofut (gofid), softened after o. yn y gwyd 'in their presence': y 'their' does not mutate gwyd. a gewssynt 'that they had got', suffered: kawssynt, pluperfect of kaffael, softened after a. e hun 'themselves'. ny doy gof 'there came no memory': doy is doei, imperfect of dyuot; gof ← cof, softened as the subject straight after the verb. o alar 'of grief' ← galar after o.

sentences.t: Ac yno y treulyssant y pedwarugeint mlyned hyt na wybuant wy eiryoet dwyn yspeit digriuach na hyurydach no honno.
sentences.l: And there they-spent the four-score years so-that they-did-not-know they ever bearing a-while more-pleasant nor more-delightful than that.
sentences.i: And there they passed the fourscore years, and never knew a time more pleasant or more delightful than that.
sentences.n: y treulyssant 'they spent', 3 pl. preterite of treulaw, as in the last part. hyt na 'so that not'. wybuant ← gwybuant, 3 pl. preterite of gwybot, softened after na. dwyn yspeit 'to pass a space of time': dwyn 'carry, bear', as of the year Branwen 'bore' in the last part; yspeit 'space, while'. digriuach, hyurydach: comparatives in -ach of digrif 'pleasant' and hyfryd 'delightful' (u = f). no honno 'than that one'.

sentences.t: Nyt oed anesmwythach, nac adnabot o un ar y gilyd y uot yn hynny o amser, no fan doethan yno.
sentences.l: There-was-not more-uneasy, nor recognising by one on the other his being in that-much of time, than when they-came there.
sentences.i: They were no more ill at ease, nor could one see on another that he had been there all that while, than when they first came.
sentences.n: Nyt oed anesmwythach 'it was not more uneasy': anesmwyth 'uneasy, comfortless' (an- + esmwyth 'ease'), with the comparative -ach. nac adnabot o un ar y gilyd 'nor any one's recognising on the other': the subject with o; y gilyd 'the other'. y uot 'his being', that he had been: bot softened after y 'his'. yn hynny o amser 'in that much of time', all that while. no fan doethan 'than when they came': fan is phan, pan with the spirant after no 'than'; doethan is doethant with its -t not written (the Red Book doethant).

sentences.t: Nit oed anesmwythach ganthunt wynte gyduot y penn yna, no phan uuassei Uendigeiduran yn uyw gyd ac wynt.
sentences.l: Was-not more-uneasy with-them they-for-their-part being-together-with the head there, than when Bendigeidfran had-been alive with them.
sentences.i: Nor did it trouble them more to have the head there with them than when Bendigeidfran had been alive among them.
sentences.n: Nit oed is nyt oed, spelt with i. wynte is wynteu. gyduot ← kyduot 'being together (with)', softened (the Red Book gytuot); with y penn it is 'being in the head's company'. yna 'there'. no phan 'than when': pan with the spirant after no, written ph this time. uuassei 'had been': buassei, the pluperfect of bot, softened after pan. yn uyw 'alive', byw softened after yn. gyd ac is gyt ac 'with', -d for -t.

sentences.t: Ac o achaws y pedwarugeint mlyned hynny y gelwit Yspydawt Urdaul Benn.
sentences.l: And because-of those four-score years it-was-called the Hospitality of-the-Honoured Head.
sentences.i: And because of those fourscore years it was called the Hospitality of the Honoured Head.
sentences.n: o achaws 'because of': the phrase first, so the verb takes y. y gelwit 'it was called': gelwit, impersonal imperfect of galw. Yspydawt Urdaul Benn names the sojourn as a tale: yspydawt 'hospitality, entertainment, feast'; urdaul 'honoured, dignified' (urddol, from urdd 'order, dignity'; the Red Book urdawl); benn ← penn, softened after the adjective set before it. Whether yspydawt here means the hospitality given, a feast, or the company kept is disputed.

sentences.t: Yspydawt Uranwen a Matholwch oed yr honn yd aethpwyt e Iwerdon.
sentences.l: The Hospitality of-Branwen and Matholwch was the one that was-gone to Ireland.
sentences.i: (The Hospitality of Branwen and Matholwch was the one when men went to Ireland.)
sentences.n: An aside, telling two tales of the same kind apart: the other 'hospitality' was the one in Ireland. The second witness puts the sentence in braces as an editor's addition, but Evans prints it as running text, and the Red Book has it too, so it stands as text; the English gives it brackets. Uranwen ← Branwen, softened after the feminine noun yspydawt. yr honn 'the one', feminine to agree. yd aethpwyt 'there was a going': impersonal preterite of mynet, 'when men went'. e Iwerdon 'to Ireland', e = y 'to'.

sentences.t: Sef a wnaeth Heilyn uab Guyn dydgueith: “Meuyl ar uy maryf i,” heb ef, “onyt agoraf y drws, e wybot ay gwir a dywedir am hynny.”
sentences.l: That-is what Heilyn son of-Gwyn did one-day: “Shame on my beard I,” said he, “unless I-open the door, to know whether true what is-said about that.”
sentences.i: One day Heilyn son of Gwyn spoke up. “Shame on my beard,” he said, “if I do not open the door, to know whether what is said of it is true.”
sentences.n: Sef a wnaeth 'that is what … did', here answered by a speech instead of verbal nouns. Guyn is Gwyn (gu = gw), the Gwyn Hen of the list. dydgueith 'one day'. Meuyl ar uy maryf i 'shame on my beard': the house oath meuyl, here with ar; maryf ← baryf, the nasal mutation after uy (b > m). onyt agoraf 'if I do not open'. e wybot 'to know': gwybot softened after e = y 'to'. ay gwir 'whether (it is) true'. a dywedir 'what is said': dywedir, present impersonal (-ir) of dywedut.

sentences.t: Agori y drws a wnaeth, ac edrych ar Gernyw, ac ar Aber Henueleu.
sentences.l: Opening the door he-did, and looking on Cornwall, and on Aber Henfelen.
sentences.i: He opened the door and looked out on Cornwall and on Aber Henfelen.
sentences.n: Agori y drws a wnaeth 'opening the door he did': the verbal noun put first and closed by a wnaeth; ac edrych 'and looking' carries on under the same subject without a verb of its own. ar Gernyw: Kernyw softened after ar. Aber Henueleu as written, as in Bendigeidfran's charge; the Red Book here has henuelen. The prohibition broken, the next sentence turns at once.

sentences.t: A phan edrychwys, yd oed yn gyn hyspysset ganthunt y gyniuer collet a gollyssynt eiryoet, a'r gyniuer car a chedymdeith a gollyssynt, a'r gyniuer drwc a dothoed udunt, a chyt bei yno y kyuarffei ac wynt; ac yn benhaf oll am eu harglwyd.
sentences.l: And when he-looked, there-was as clear with-them every loss they-had-lost ever, and every kinsman and companion that they-had-lost, and every evil that had-come to-them, as-if there it-were that it-met them; and chiefest of-all about their lord.
sentences.i: And when he looked, every loss they had ever suffered, every kinsman and comrade they had lost, and every ill that had come upon them, was as plain to them as if it were meeting them there and then; and above all, the loss of their lord.
sentences.n: edrychwys 'looked', 3 sg. -wys preterite. yn gyn hyspysset 'as clear': kyn 'as' softened after yn, with hyspysset, the equative of hyspys 'clear, known'. y gyniuer 'every … that, as many as': kyniuer softened after the article. gollyssynt ← collyssynt, pluperfect, softened after a. car 'kinsman, friend'; a chedymdeith ← kedymdeith 'companion', the spirant after a. dothoed 'had come', pluperfect of dyuot. a chyt bei yno y kyuarffei ac wynt 'as if it were there that it met them': kyt 'though, as if'; bei and kyuarffei are imperfect subjunctives (kyuaruot 'meet'). yn benhaf ← pennaf. eu harglwyd: h before a vowel after eu 'their'.

sentences.t: Ac o'r gyuawr honno, ny allyssant wy orfowys namyn kychu a'r penn parth a Llundein.
sentences.l: And from that very-hour, they-could-not they rest but [make-for] with the head towards London.
sentences.i: And from that hour they could not rest, but set off with the head for London.
sentences.n: o'r gyuawr honno 'from that very hour': kyuawr softened after the article (feminine). ny allyssant ← gallyssant, 3 pl. preterite of gallu, softened after ny, the g lost. orfowys ← gorfowys, softened as the object. namyn 'but'. kychu: so Evans prints, certain on the image. The second witness reads kyrchu 'make for', the Red Book kychwynnu ar penn 'set out with the head'. kychu is not a known word: it is kept as printed, as a slip either for kyrchu or for a shortened kychwynu; which one is uncertain, but either way they go on with the head towards London.

sentences.t: Pa hyt bynnac y bydynt ar y ford, wynt a doethant hyt yn Llundein, ac a gladyssant y penn yn y Gwynuryn.
sentences.l: However long they-would-be on the road, they it-was-that came as-far-as into London, and buried the head in the White-Hill.
sentences.i: However long they were on the road, they came to London and buried the head in the White Hill.
sentences.n: Pa hyt bynnac 'however long': pa hyt 'what length' + bynnac '-ever'. y bydynt 'they were', the habitual past of bot, as bydynt above. wynt a doethant 'they came', the abnormal sentence. a gladyssant 'buried': cladyssant, 3 pl. preterite, softened after a. yn y Gwynuryn, as Bendigeidfran had ordered. The tale tells nothing of the road; the journey ends in one sentence.

sentences.t: A hwnnw trydyd matcud ban gudywyt, a'r trydyd anuat datcud pann datcudywyt; cany doey ormes byth drwy uor y'r ynys honn, tra uei y penn yn y cud hwnnw.
sentences.l: And that-one third fortunate-concealment when it-was-concealed, and the third unfortunate disclosure when it-was-disclosed; since there-would-not-come oppression ever across sea to this island, while was the head in that concealment.
sentences.i: And that was the third Fortunate Concealment when it was concealed, and the third Unfortunate Disclosure when it was disclosed; for no oppression would ever come across the sea to this island while the head lay in that concealment.
sentences.n: There is no verb: A hwnnw trydyd matcud 'and that (was the) third …'; the Red Book has a hwnnw uu y trydyd. The tale quotes a triad, the 'Three Fortunate Concealments' with the 'Three Unfortunate Disclosures': matcud is mat 'good, fortunate' + cud 'hiding'; anuat datcud is 'unfortunate (anfad) uncovering'. The other members are not named here, and whether mat and anuat mean 'fortunate, unfortunate' or 'good, evil' is disputed. ban gudywyt 'when it was hidden': cudywyt, impersonal preterite, softened after ban; datcudywyt likewise. cany 'since … not'. doey, imperfect of dyuot. ormes ← gormes 'oppression', softened as the subject after the verb. drwy uor ← mor after drwy. tra uei 'while it was'.

sentences.t: A hynny a dyweit y kyuarwydyd hwnn.
sentences.l: And that it-is-that this tale says.
sentences.i: And that is what this tale tells.
sentences.n: A hynny a dyweit 'and that is what … says': hynny put first, the abnormal sentence; dyweit, 3 sg. present of dywedut. y kyuarwydyd hwnn 'this tale': kyuarwydyd 'lore, guidance, story', the matter a kyuarwyd (storyteller) knows. In the Red Book this sentence runs straight on into the next (y kyuarwydyt eu kyfranc hwy, 'the tale (of) their adventure'); the full stop here is our punctuation, and the two sentences may be one.

sentences.t: Eu kyfranc wy, “Y gwyr a gychwynwys o Iwerdon,” yw hwnnw.
sentences.l: Their adventure they, “The men that set-out from Ireland,” is that.
sentences.i: Their adventure is the one called “The Men Who Set Out from Ireland.”
sentences.n: kyfranc 'encounter, adventure', and so a tale of one. Eu … wy 'their', with the pronoun repeated after the noun. Y gwyr a gychwynwys o Iwerdon 'the men who set out from Ireland' is a tale-title, so it is quoted: a gychwynwys ← kychwynwys, -wys preterite, softened after a, and singular after the relative though the men are plural. yw hwnnw 'is that one': yw, the 'is' used when the predicate comes first. With the next paragraph the tale turns back to Ireland.

sentences.t: En Iwerdon nyt edewit dyn byw, namyn pump gwraged beichawc y mywn gogof yn diffeithwch Iwerdon.
sentences.l: In Ireland was-not-left a-person alive, except five women pregnant in a cave in the wilderness of-Ireland.
sentences.i: In Ireland not a living soul was left, save five women with child in a cave in the wilds of Ireland.
sentences.n: En is yn 'in'. nyt edewit 'there was not left': edewit, impersonal preterite of adaw, as in the last part. dyn byw 'a living person'. pump gwraged 'five women': gwraged is plural, where a numeral usually takes the singular noun (pump gwreic); the Red Book has the same. beichawc 'pregnant'. y mywn gogof 'in a cave', our word division as before. diffeithwch 'wilderness', from diffeith 'waste', the word of Branwen's lament (diffeithwyt).

sentences.t: A'r pump wraged hynny, yn yr un kyfnot, a anet udunt pum meib.
sentences.l: And those five women, in the same time, were-born to-them five sons.
sentences.i: And to those five women, at one and the same time, five sons were born.
sentences.n: The sentence changes course: 'those five women … there were born to them five sons', the women set out first and then taken up by udunt 'to them'. wraged here is softened after pump (the Red Book gwraged); the softening has no clear cause. yn yr un kyfnot 'in the same time' (kyfnod). a anet 'were born': ganet, impersonal preterite of geni, softened after a, the g dropping away, as of Gwern in the last part. pum meib 'five sons': pump becomes pum before a noun, and the noun is again plural.

sentences.t: A'r pym meib hynny a uagyssant hyt ban uuant weisson mawr, ac yny uedylyssant am wraged, ac yny uu damunet gantunt eu cafael.
sentences.l: And those five sons it-was-that were-reared until they-were lads big, and until they-thought about women, and until was desire with-them their getting.
sentences.i: And those five sons were reared until they were grown youths, and thought of women, and wanted to have them.
sentences.n: pym meib: pump again, spelt pym. a uagyssant: magyssant, 3 pl. preterite of magu 'rear', softened after a. With the sons as subject it must mean 'were reared, grew up', unless the mothers are the subject and the sons the object set first; the construction is loose. hyt ban uuant 'until they were': buant softened after ban. weisson mawr 'big lads' ← gweisson, softened as the predicate. yny uedylyssant 'until they thought': medylyssant, softened after yny. damunet 'desire'. eu cafael 'their getting', to have them: cafael is kaffael, eu 'them' its object.

sentences.t: Ac yna, kyscu pob un lau heb lau gan uam y gilid, a gwledychu y wlat a'y chyuanhedu, a'y rannu y rydunt yll pymp.
sentences.l: And then, sleeping each one hand past hand with the mother of the other, and ruling the land and its peopling, and its dividing between-them all five.
sentences.i: And then each in turn lay with another's mother, and they ruled the land and peopled it, and divided it among the five of them.
sentences.n: kyscu … gan 'sleeping with'. lau heb lau 'hand past hand', in turn: llaw softened as an adverb (ll > l), with u for w; the Red Book law heb law. gan uam y gilid 'with the mother of the other': mam softened after gan. gwledychu 'ruling'. y wlat ← gwlat after the article. a'y chyuanhedu 'and its peopling': 'y 'its' (fem., for gwlat) gives the spirant, kyuanhedu > chyuanhedu; in a'y rannu 'and its dividing' r has no spirant to show. y rydunt 'between them' (rwng conjugated, 3 pl.), as in the last part. yll pymp 'the five of them'.

sentences.t: Ac o achaws y ranyat hwnnw y gelwir etwan pymp rann Ywerdon.
sentences.l: And because-of that division are-called still the five parts of-Ireland.
sentences.i: And because of that division men still speak of the five parts of Ireland.
sentences.n: y ranyat hwnnw 'that division': ranyat is rhaniad, r written for rh; it is masculine, so unchanged after the article. y gelwir 'are called': gelwir, present impersonal (-ir) of galw. etwan 'still', a by-form of etwa (as in the last part). pymp rann Ywerdon 'the five parts of Ireland', the five provinces of Irish tradition (the Red Book pump rann iwerdon). Ywerdon is Iwerdon spelt with y. The tale gives the origin of a name, as with Seith Marchawc in the last part.

sentences.t: Ac edrych y wlat a wnaethant ford y buassei yr aeruaeu, a chael eur, ac aryant, yny ytoedynt yn gyuoethawc.
sentences.l: And examining the land they-did where had-been the battlefields, and getting gold, and silver, until they-were rich.
sentences.i: And they searched the land where the battlefields had been, and found gold and silver, until they were rich.
sentences.n: edrych … a wnaethant 'examining they did', the verbal-noun pattern with y wlat as its object. ford y 'the way that', where: ffordd, f for ff. buassei 'had been', pluperfect of bot, singular before a plural noun subject. aeruaeu 'battlefields': aer 'battle, slaughter' + maeu 'fields', softened in the compound. a chael 'and getting', the spirant after a. yny ytoedynt 'until they were': ytoedynt is yd oedynt, the particle and the 3 pl. imperfect of bot written together. yn gyuoethawc 'rich' ← kyuoethawc, softened after yn; the word is from kyuoeth 'realm, wealth'.

sentences.t: A llyna ual y teruyna y geing honn o'r Mabinyogi, o achaws Paluawt Branwen, yr honn a uu tryded anuat paluawt yn yr ynys honn;
sentences.l: And there-is how ends this branch of the Mabinogi, because-of the Blow of-Branwen, which was third unfortunate blow in this island;
sentences.i: And so ends this branch of the Mabinogi, concerning the Blow of Branwen, which was the third Unfortunate Blow in this island;
sentences.n: A llyna ual 'and that is how': the closing formula. teruyna 'ends', 3 sg. present of teruynu. y geing honn 'this branch': keing (keinc) softened after the article, being feminine. Mabinyogi is Mabinogi spelt with y. o achaws 'because of', here 'concerning': the branch names the tales it holds. Paluawt Branwen 'the Blow of Branwen': paluawt 'a blow with the open hand' (palf 'palm'), the butcher's daily box on the ear. tryded anuat paluawt 'the third Unfortunate Blow', another triad; tryded is the feminine 'third'. The sense of anuat here, as with the Disclosure above, is disputed.

sentences.t: ac o achaws Yspadawt Uran, pan aeth yniuer pedeir decwlat a seithugeint e Iwerdon, y dial Paluawt Branwen; ac am y ginyaw yn Hardlech seith mlyned; ac am Ganyat Adar Riannon; ac ar Yspydaut Benn pedwarugeint mlyned.
sentences.l: and because-of the Hospitality of-Brân, when went the host of-four ten-lands and seven-score to Ireland, to avenge the Blow of-Branwen; and about the dinner in Harlech seven years; and about the Singing of-the-Birds of-Rhiannon; and on the Hospitality of-the-Head four-score years.
sentences.i: and concerning the Hospitality of Brân, when the host of the seven score and fourteen lands went to Ireland to avenge the Blow of Branwen; and the seven years' feast at Harlech; and the Singing of the Birds of Rhiannon; and the fourscore years' Hospitality of the Head.
sentences.n: So ends the Second Branch, Branwen, naming its tales: Paluawt Branwen 'the Blow of Branwen'; Yspadawt Uran 'the Hospitality of Brân' (yspadawt is yspydawt; Uran ← Bran after the feminine noun); the Ginyaw yn Hardlech 'the Feast at Harlech' (y ginyaw softened after the article as if feminine, though kinyaw is usually masculine; the Red Book has the same); Canyat Adar Riannon 'the Singing of the Birds of Rhiannon' (canyat softened after am); and Yspydaut Benn 'the Hospitality of the Head' (u for w). pedeir decwlat a seithugeint is the count of the last part, read as 154 lands; the Red Book here has deg wlat a seith ugeint 'ten lands and seven score', 150. y dial 'to avenge'. ac ar Yspydaut: Evans prints ar where am 'about' would be expected; the second witness reads am, but the Red Book also has ar, so ar is kept.
